questions.q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated in ethanol. The major alkene formed is:
questions.explain: The tertiary carbocation loses H⁺ from the CH₂ to give the trisubstituted (Saytzeff) alkene; loss from a CH₃ gives the minor 2-methylbut-1-ene.

questions.q: In an E1 reaction of a tertiary alkyl bromide, the concentration of the weak base is doubled. The rate:
questions.explain: Rate = k[RX]: only the substrate is involved in the slow ionisation step, so the base does not appear in the rate law.

questions.q: Which statement about the E1 mechanism is NOT correct?
options: Hydride or alkyl shifts can occur before deprotonation
SN1 products often form alongside the alkene
The β-H and the leaving group must be anti-periplanar
questions.explain: The β-H is removed from a free planar carbocation after the leaving group has gone, so no anti-periplanar arrangement is needed; that requirement belongs to E2.

questions.q: (CH₃)₃C–Br and (CD₃)₃C–Br are each heated in ethanol and eliminate by E1 at nearly the same rate. The best explanation is:
options: The C–H (or C–D) bond breaks only after the rate-determining ionisation
C–D and C–H bonds have equal strength
Deuterium makes the carbocation less stable
The C–H bond breaks in the slow step, together with the C–Br bond
questions.explain: The slow step is loss of Br⁻ to form the carbocation, and the C–H bond breaks later in the fast deprotonation, so there is no significant primary deuterium isotope effect.
